673.title: The winter solstice
673.hook: the longest night, and the light returns from here
673.howItsDone: Several traditions hold festivals of light around the winter solstice, each with its own meaning; some people mark the longest night simply by lighting a candle and keeping company.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Saturnalia, when masters served and Seneca kept a sober head. Your line was roles reversed.

Four-thirty in the afternoon and it's already dark. You leave work in the dark; you might have arrived in it too. In the far north, the sun barely clears the horizon, or doesn't rise at all. And yet, all around the world, this darkest stretch of the year is full of lights. Strings of them on houses. Candles in windows. In Iran, families stay up through Yalda, the longest night, eating pomegranates and reading poetry. Other traditions keep their own festivals of light around now, each with its own meaning. Today: the winter solstice.
screen: `DARK AT FOUR-THIRTY.` → `CANDLES IN WINDOWS.` → `THE LONGEST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the turn at the bottom. At the summer solstice, the peak of the light was also the start of its going. Now it's the mirror: the longest night is the moment the light starts coming back. Tomorrow will be a little longer than today, though nobody will notice at first. Second, Seneca on the seasons. In one letter he tells Lucilius that the world itself runs on change. Winter brings the cold, and we have to shiver. Summer brings the heat, and we have to sweat. We can't change that order, he says, but we can take on a great spirit, worthy of a good person, and bear what comes bravely, in agreement with nature. The dark isn't a punishment. It's part of the turning. Third, a Stoic and his lamp. Epictetus tells his students he once had an iron lamp by his household gods, and a thief stole it. Tomorrow, he says, I'll buy a clay one. And the thief paid a higher price: to get the lamp, he agreed to become a thief. A lamp can be replaced. What Epictetus chooses to be cannot be stolen. Fourth, why a candle. A candle in the dark doesn't argue with the night or make it day. It just makes a small circle where you can see a face, a page, your own hands. Getting through a hard season often looks like that: not ending the dark, but keeping one small light going until the days lengthen on their own.
screen: `THE LONGEST NIGHT IS ALSO THE TURN.` · `WINTER BRINGS COLD: WE SHIVER.` · `EPICTETUS'S STOLEN LAMP.` · `A SMALL CIRCLE OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Light a candle safely, or turn on one small lamp and turn the others off, and notice how far the light reaches and where the dark begins. Don't push the dark away; let the small light be enough. Then hold in mind one person who's in a dark season right now, inside this small circle of light.
Winter solstice, the longest night of the year, and the turning point after which the light returns, little by little. Today's word.
Your line: the light returns. Little by little, whether anyone notices or not. Day six hundred seventy-three.

674.title: A Stoic birthday
674.hook: Seneca would ask: how much of this past year did you really live?
674.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca use a birthday or new year to review how much of the past year they truly lived, and what they want more of in the next.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was winter solstice, the longest night and the turn toward light. Your line was the light returns.

Candles on a cake. Someone counts them, or gives up and uses a number-shaped candle instead. Thirty-four. Fifty-two. Seventy-one. Everyone sings, slightly off key, and somebody says: another year older! The number is the headline of a birthday. But Seneca, who wrote a whole essay about how we spend our time, would lean across the table, very politely, and ask a different question. Not how many years. How much of this past year did you actually live?
screen: `CANDLES ON A CAKE.` → `ANOTHER YEAR OLDER!` → `HOW MUCH DID YOU LIVE?`

segments.voice: First, the essay. Seneca's On the Shortness of Life, written to a friend named Paulinus, opens with a complaint everyone makes: life is too short. Seneca disagrees. Life is long enough, he says, if we use it well. It's we who make it short, by wasting it. Second, the audit. Imagine an old man, he says, and add up his years honestly. How many went to a demanding boss, to quarrels, to errands around the city, to worries he invented, to things he didn't even enjoy? Take those away, and he has far fewer years than he counts. Third, the sharpest line. Don't think someone has lived long because of gray hair and wrinkles. That person hasn't lived long; they've been around long. It's like a sailor caught in a storm the moment he leaves the harbor, blown in circles for days. He didn't have a long voyage. He was just tossed about a lot. Fourth, a birthday on the porch. Seneca isn't asking for guilt. He's asking for an honest count. Which days this past year were actually lived, with attention, with people, with something that mattered? Those count. The others aren't failures; they're information. A birthday is a good day to ask, because the next year hasn't been spent yet.
screen: `LIFE IS LONG, IF YOU USE IT.` · `SUBTRACT THE WASTED YEARS.` · `NOT LIVED LONG: AROUND LONG.` · `AN HONEST COUNT, NOT GUILT.` · then, large: `HOW MUCH DID I LIVE?`

segments.voice: Whether it's your birthday or not, look back over the last twelve months and find three moments when you were fully alive, present with people or work or a place that mattered, and let them count. Then gently notice one stretch that slipped away, scrolling, worrying, rushing, with no blame. Ask what you'd want more of, and less of, in the year ahead.

675.title: The Stoic morning
675.hook: preview, one principle, and a clear intention
675.howItsDone: Some modern Stoic practitioners begin the day with a short routine drawn from Marcus and Epictetus: previewing difficulties, recalling one principle, and setting an intention.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Paulinus, the friend Seneca wrote to about the shortness of life. Your line was how much did I live.

The alarm goes off, and the phone is already in reach. Before feet touch the floor, a thumb is scrolling: messages, headlines, someone's vacation, a work email marked urgent. A minute or two in, the day's mood has been set by whoever got there first. The turning year is done. For the next stretch, the porch puts a year of Stoic reading to work in ordinary life: morning, evening, work, home, the hard days and the good ones. It starts where every day starts.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE PHONE, THE HEADLINES.` → `DECIDED BY WHOEVER GOT THERE FIRST.` → `LIVING THE PORCH BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Three parts, gathered mostly from Marcus. First, preview. Marcus opens book two of his notebook with this, in George Long's 1862 translation: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." It sounds grim. But read on: none of them can really harm him, he says, and they're his kin, made for working together. The preview isn't pessimism. It's packing an umbrella: when the rude email comes, you've already met it once, calmly. Second, one principle. Marcus tells himself to keep his principles ready the way a doctor keeps instruments at hand for sudden cases. Not a whole philosophy. One line for the day: maybe Epictetus's split, some things are up to me, some aren't, or Seneca's begin now, or one you've written yourself. Third, intention. On a morning Marcus didn't want to get up, he asked himself what he was made for: to lie under the blankets keeping warm, or to do the work of a human being? An intention answers that for today. Not a to-do list. A how: patient with my kids, honest in the meeting, kind on the phone. Fourth, the whole thing takes about two minutes. Preview, principle, intention, before the phone if you can. The day will still surprise you, but you'll meet it as yourself, not as whoever the first notification decided you'd be.
screen: `PREVIEW: MEET THE DAY ONCE, CALMLY.` · `ONE PRINCIPLE, READY AT HAND.` · `INTENTION: THE WORK OF A HUMAN BEING.` · `TWO MINUTES, BEFORE THE PHONE.` · then, large: `PREVIEW, PRINCIPLE, INTENTION.`

segments.voice: Try a Stoic morning now, whatever the hour: picture the rest of your day and meet its likely friction once, calmly. Choose one line to carry and say it silently. Then finish this sentence for yourself, today I want to be someone who, and let all three settle.
Stoic morning: a two-minute start, preview the day, choose one principle, set a clear intention, before the world decides for you. Today's word.
Your line: preview, principle, intention. Two minutes, and the day starts as yours. Day six hundred seventy-five, done.

676.title: The Stoic evening
676.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners end the day with a short review modeled on Seneca and Sextius: what went well, where they slipped, how they grew, followed by self-forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Stoic morning: preview, principle, intention. Today, the other end of the day.

Lights out. The head hits the pillow, and the replay starts on its own. The thing you said in the meeting. The text you didn't answer. The way you snapped at your partner over the dishes. Round and round, the loop that keeps people awake. Seneca had a different way of ending the day. It took a few minutes, it happened on purpose, and it ended with something like a pardon. He borrowed it from an older philosopher, and he described it in his essay On Anger.
screen: `LIGHTS OUT, THE REPLAY STARTS.` → `THE LOOP THAT KEEPS YOU UP.` → `A REVIEW ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, where Seneca got it. The philosopher Sextius, he tells us, would question his own mind at the end of each day, before sleep. Three questions. What bad habit have you healed today? What fault have you resisted? In what way are you better? Second, older roots. The Pythagoreans had verses asking something similar each night: where did I go wrong? What did I do? What duty did I leave undone? Epictetus quotes those lines to his students. In Greek the first question is pē parebēn: where did I step aside? Third, how Seneca does it. When the lamp is out, and his wife, who knows his habit, has gone quiet, he goes over his whole day, every word and deed, hiding nothing from himself and skipping nothing. Then an example: in that argument, you spoke too sharply; don't argue with people who can't be taught. And the verdict: see that you don't do it again. This time, I forgive you. Fourth, why gently matters. The bedtime replay and the Stoic review look alike, but they work in opposite directions. The replay is a loop: same scene, more anxiety, no ending. The review is a line: look, learn one thing, forgive, close the file. Sleep after it is especially sweet, Seneca says, because the mind has been praised or warned and knows where it stands.
screen: `SEXTIUS'S THREE QUESTIONS.` · `PĒ PAREBĒN: WHERE DID I GO WRONG?` · `THIS TIME, I FORGIVE YOU.` · `A LINE, NOT A LOOP.` · then, large: `THREE QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Run a short evening review now: what habit did you resist today, where did you slip, and in what way were you better, even slightly? Let one honest answer come to each, without arguing for or against yourself. Then, if it helps, say Seneca's verdict silently: don't do it again; this time, I forgive you.
Stoic evening: Seneca's nightly review, three honest questions about the day, and then a gentle pardon so you can sleep. Today's word.
Your line: three questions. Then the file closes, and the day can go. Sleep well.

677.title: Stoic at work
677.hook: duties, roles, and control at work
677.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners sort work worries into what is and isn't up to them, then give full effort to their own part and the duties of their role.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Stoic evening: Sextius's questions and Seneca's pardon. Your line was three questions.

Sunday night, around eight. The feeling arrives on schedule: the project that's behind, the manager who's hard to read, the rumor about layoffs, the colleague who takes credit. Some of it is real work. Some of it is weather. All of it lands in the same knot in your stomach. The Stoics didn't have open-plan offices. But many of Epictetus's students were young men headed for posts in public life, and Marcus wrote his notebook while hearing cases and running campaigns. They had a lot to say about doing work without letting it own you.
screen: `SUNDAY NIGHT, EIGHT O'CLOCK.` → `REAL WORK, AND WEATHER.` → `ONE KNOT IN THE STOMACH.`

segments.voice: First, the split. The Handbook opens with it: some things are up to us, and some are not. At work, that sorts quickly. Up to you: how carefully you do the task, how honestly you speak, how you treat the people around you, whether you ask for help. Not up to you: the budget, the reorganization, whether your manager likes your idea, the economy. Second, roles. You met this idea with Cicero a month ago; Epictetus puts it in one line: our duties are measured by our relationships. You're a colleague, so act as a good colleague. You're someone's manager, or someone's report: ask what that role asks of you, today, at this desk. Third, the Stoic word. Kathēkon: an appropriate action, the fitting thing for someone in your place to do. It isn't heroic. It's the email answered clearly, the meeting attended fully, the mistake owned up to. Fourth, together. A lot of work worry comes from mixing the two columns: carrying the layoff rumor as if it were your task, or treating your own sloppy report as if it were fate. Sort them, and the knot loosens a little. The first column gets your full effort. The second gets your attention, maybe your preparation, but not your sleep. Marcus reminded himself more than once to do the thing in front of him with simple dignity, as if it were the last thing he would ever do.
screen: `UP TO ME, NOT UP TO ME.` · `DUTIES MEASURED BY ROLES.` · `KATHĒKON: THE FITTING THING.` · `TWO COLUMNS, ONE KNOT LOOSENED.` · then, large: `MY PART AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Bring one worry from work, school, volunteering or caregiving to mind, and picture a page with two columns. On the left, up to me: what you can actually do; on the right, not up to me: what you can't control, and let those stay there. Look at the left column only, and let one thing from it stand out.
Kathēkon, the Stoic word for the fitting action: doing your role's appropriate part fully, and leaving what isn't up to you in its own column. Today's word.
Your line: my part at work. The fitting thing is usually a small one. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

678.title: Stoic at home
678.hook: the hive, the household, the people you live with
678.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat the household as the first circle of their care, doing small unasked tasks for the people they live with without keeping score.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kathēkon, the fitting thing. Your line was my part at work: two columns, and the knot loosens.

The sink has a pan in it that's been soaking since Tuesday. Nobody remembers whose it is. It's become a sort of household monument. Everyone walks past it. Everyone has an opinion about it. Nobody touches it. If you've lived with roommates, a partner, kids or parents, you know this pan, or its cousin, the empty toilet paper roll. It can be oddly hard to be patient and good in the place where we're most ourselves. The Stoics thought home was exactly where philosophy gets tested.
screen: `THE PAN SOAKING SINCE TUESDAY.` → `EVERYONE WALKS PAST IT.` → `WHERE PHILOSOPHY GETS TESTED.`

segments.voice: First, the hive. Marcus Aurelius writes, in George Long's 1862 translation: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee." A bee doesn't thrive by doing well while the hive falls apart. Whatever helps only me, at the expense of the people I live with, isn't really good for me either. Second, the circles. A later Stoic named Hierocles drew a picture: you at the center of a set of circles. The first ring is your own mind and body. The next is your closest family, then your wider family, neighbors, your town, and finally all of humanity. The task, he says, is to draw the circles inward, treating the people in each ring a little more like the ones closer in. The household is the very first ring past your own skin. Third, the word underneath. Oikeiōsis: making something your own, belonging. It comes from oikos, the Greek word for household. For the Stoics, care starts with what is closest and grows outward. Home isn't a break from virtue; it's the first ring it has to cross. Fourth, the pan. A Stoic at home isn't someone who never gets annoyed. It's someone who asks what's good for the hive, and then does one small thing for it without keeping score. Wash the pan. Replace the roll. Not as a martyr, not to make a point. Just as a bee who knows where it lives.
screen: `NOT GOOD FOR THE SWARM, NOR THE BEE.` · `HIEROCLES' CIRCLES, DRAWN INWARD.` · `OIKEIŌSIS: FROM OIKOS, HOUSEHOLD.` · `ONE THING FOR THE HIVE, NO SCORE.` · then, large: `FOR THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Picture your home and the people in it, or if you live alone, the people closest to you, with you in the middle and them in the first ring. Notice whether any score is being kept, about chores or who gives more, without blame. Then let one small, unasked-for thing you could do for the house come to mind.
Oikeiōsis, the Stoic word for making something your own: the household as the hive and the first circle past your own skin. Today's word.

679.title: Stoic in grief
679.hook: honest grief, the seasons, sweet memory
679.howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca treat grief as something to feel honestly rather than suppress, and over time to turn into grateful memory of the person lost.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was oikeiōsis, the household as the hive and your first circle. Your line was for the house.

Someone at the funeral says it to the dead man's daughter, meaning well: you're being so strong. She hasn't cried in front of anyone. She went back to work on Monday. People admire it. And at two in the morning, alone in her kitchen, it isn't strength at all. It's a held breath. That's the common picture of Stoic grief: a stiff upper lip, nothing shown. Seneca's letters paint a different one.
screen: `YOU'RE BEING SO STRONG.` → `TWO A.M., A HELD BREATH.` → `WHAT SENECA'S GRIEF LOOKS LIKE.`

segments.voice: Three threads, held together. First, honest grief. Seneca, writing to Lucilius after a friend's death, doesn't tell him not to cry. The eyes shouldn't be dry when a friend is lost, he says, nor should they overflow: tears are allowed, wailing isn't required. Then he confesses that when his own friend Annaeus Serenus died, he wept beyond all measure, and counts himself among those whom grief defeated. A teacher who admits that is not asking for stone. Second, the seasons. The Stoics placed death inside nature's turning, like the ripe olive. That doesn't cancel sorrow. It's a frame big enough to hold it: leaves fall, and you still miss the green. Seneca, writing to a mother three years into mourning her son, is gentle and patient, and also asks her, slowly, to let her life go on. Third, sweet memory. Seneca passes on a saying from his teacher Attalus: remembering lost friends can be pleasant, the way some fruits are good because they're a little sharp, or a very old wine has a bitterness that pleases. Seneca's hope is that the memory of those we've lost becomes a joy, not only a wound. Put together: tears when they come, a loss held inside the turning year, and, over time, the person coming back as a memory you can visit with something like gladness. Not instead of sorrow. Alongside it. And today closes a week of carrying the porch into ordinary days.
screen: `EYES NOT DRY, NOT OVERFLOWING.` · `SENECA WEPT BEYOND MEASURE.` · `A FRAME BIG ENOUGH FOR SORROW.` · `MEMORY, SHARP AND SWEET.` · then, large: `GRIEF, HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one loss, a person, an animal, a place, a time of life, choosing one that feels bearable today; you don't have to open the hardest door. Let yourself feel what's there, honestly, then let one specific memory come, a voice, a joke, a meal, and hold it like a sharp, sweet fruit. If tears come, they're welcome here; if they don't, that's fine too.
Attalus, the teacher whose saying Seneca passed on: that remembering lost friends can turn sweet, like a good bitterness, over time. Today's word.
Your line: grief, honestly. Tears and gladness can share the same memory. See you tomorrow.
